text: Federer Nadal and Djokovic had long-term stable partners throughout their primes. Federer met Mirka in 2000 and married her in 2009. Nadal began with Xisca around 2005 and married in 2019. Djokovic dated Jelena from ~2005 and married in 2014. These 15–20+ year relationships overlapped with their dominance.How the relationships helped They provided emotional stability amid travel pressure and injuries. Partners managed logistics and daily life freeing mental focus for tennis. Continuity removed major personal distractions during peak years. The maturity required reinforced the discipline needed for long careers. All three publicly credited their partners for support and longevity. Why Sinner and Alcaraz lack the same advantage They are younger and still early in their peak years. Sinner’s relationships (Braccini Kalinskaya now Hasanovic since late 2025) have been shorter and less continuous no deep emotions. Alcaraz has mostly remained single or in brief unconfirmed links and has noted the difficulty of relationships with constant travel. Their partnerships are not yet multi-decade deeply integrated support systems. Age and timing mean they do not yet have the same long-term buffer of stability the Big Three enjoyed. This is the big reason why the new Kings will not reach the levels of big 3 the life part is huge in elite top life athlete
label: hot_take

text: Recently spoke to a really helpful coach who explained why Americans are at a disadvantage when it comes to playing college tennis and also how it leads to the long term downfall of the sport. He was honest and straightforward. A. Schools offer other grants outside of athletics for foreigners . So for example if a tennis team has 4.5 scholarships for men they can use this aid to have more money for the team by choosing internationals.So if there is an excess of 11.5 utr’s it makes more sense to give that spot to an international.B. Internationals don't quit the team. Americans they recruit often times do not stick around. (This one is obvious as Americans have more and easier options. When an international has his visa tied to a school and no family nearby they are far easier to control. Not really easy to fly back home and tell your parents you hated playing there and are back to zero. So in my opinion almost like a hostage situation. More likely to play through injuries etc ) C. Top foreign recruits want to go pro. Think 13.5 to 14 utr. Their entire life has been tennis and they are better. USA colleges offers free training and top level coaching. Bare minimum time spent studying before and during college. D. More match play variety. USA is large so many players play more often in their region. Often times against the same kids. Euro kids hop on a train and play junior ITF of which they have 500 a year in Europe to choose from. USA has 32 junior ITF. E. Foreign kids don’t know the difference between Appalachian state and Georgia tech. Far easier sell for small programs. And again the Appalachian state coaches for example know the foreign kids will have a harder time just quitting or leaving. F. More independence. Foreign kids are traveling around Europe alone to play at 15-16. This is true. I also see that Japanese boys and girls take the metro alone to school at 5 years old. Not really a fault of American kids we just don’t fly them around the country alone as young teens

text: There are many myths and legends in tennis history surrounding some of the great names in the game. Some followers of the sport felt the urge to embellish or exaggerate the achievements of their heroes and in doing so they created a number of myths that have persisted over time. These myths often revolve around the players' skills personalities and off-court lives and they can sometimes overshadow the actual accomplishments of these athletes. For example some myths suggest that certain players had supernatural abilities or that they were invincible on certain surfaces when in reality their success was the result of hard work strategy and dedication. It's important to separate fact from fiction when discussing the history of tennis and to appreciate the true achievements of its legends without being swayed by myths and legends

text: I've been digging through the Match Charting Project (Jeff Sackmann's volunteer shot-by-shot charts about 11800 matches) and the Federer v Kyrgios numbers came out backwards from what I expected. For every shot you can compare where a player hit with two benchmarks from the same position and the same stroke: the direction the average tour player picks and the direction that wins the point most often. Against the average Federer chose well. He's better at it than 68% of charted ATP players. Kyrgios sits just below the middle. Against the best option it flips. Federer left 2.74 points per 100 shots on the table Kyrgios 2.66. The gap between the two of them is small enough to call a tie but about two thirds of the tour left less than Federer did. Then there's execution: how well a player hit the shot he picked. Kyrgios is in the top 5% of the tour Federer around the 72nd percentile and that gap is far bigger than the noise. My best guess is that Federer kept working his way into positions with lots of options where the gap between a good choice and the best one is widest while Kyrgios played more points where there were fewer ways to get it wrong. I'm not sure that's the whole story

text: Did Sinner tank the AO 2026 SF match? OK, look, I know that most of you will disagree with me on this, but really, Djokovic shouldn't even have been in the finals. His AO finalist plate deserves an asterisk all over it. Sinner TANKED the SF match against Djokovic. He never intended on winning that match, nor did he want to. And yet, even with Sinner going very easy on him, it took Djokovic (who was playing noticeably better in the SF than in the F) an extremely close five setter to barely "defeat" Sinner. Even then, Djokovic still won 12 points less than Sinner. Safe to say, even when Sinner was holding back and Djokovic was playing anomalously well, the two were basically on par with each other, and if anything, it was Sinner who was overall the better player. Now, what happened when this very version of Djokovic showed up in the first set of last night's finals match? He dominated Carlitos 6-2 in less than 40 minutes. It was only when his body finally started remembering it was 39 years old that Djokovic's level dropped substantially in sets 2, 3 & 4. But then, even in set 4, Carlitos just barely managed to scrape by. Let's not kid ourselves: we all know that Sinner, if he were truly going all out, would've steamrolled Djokovic in straight sets, just like he did in their last four meetings. And he would've needed 4 sets at most to dismantle a rather subpar Carlitos in the finals.

text: Federer has the last laugh vs Djokovic Djokovic may end up with more slams, but Federer has the last laugh. All of the Djokovic-style players went nowhere: Ferrer Zverev Coric Chung Goffin Nishikori The list goes on and on. These were all basliners modeled at least partially after Djokovic. They all failed to become great players (so far). The baseline-camper mindset is not a good one to have. Djokovic managed to do it with great mental strength, but that was because the mental strength came before he turned into a baseline pushbot in 2011. The other players adopted his style but never developed the mental strength, precisely because they adopted that style. It made them afraid to really go for it in big moments. They clung to their baseline camping all the way to the end. On the other hand, the one young player that actually plays like Federer is the new ATG talent. He has already outperformed all of the Djokovic bots and he is only 19. It's about mindset. Alcaraz has the fearless attacking mindset that Federer possessed, and it is exactly what is missing with all the baseline bots. It's not that he can't play from the baseline, or that he lives at the net, but it's a mentality of putting the match on your racquet and not your opponent's racquet. The spirit of Federer is still winning slams and may be the next great dominant player and ATG. The spirit of Djokovic is nowhere close - and that's a good thing. The last thing the tour needs are slam-winning *********.

text: Is Borg the GOAT if the U.S. Open stays on clay through 1981? The U.S. Open switched from grass to Har-Tru for three years from 1975-1977. Then, due to a variety of reasons, such as lower court maintenance courts, it switched venues as well as surface: from clay to hard. But what if it stayed on clay through 1981, maybe even 1982 or 1983? In 1978, I still think Connors takes the title because he was playing so well and Borg had his bad thumb injury. In 1979, Bog lost a tough four setter to Tanner when he had trouble returning the American's big serves under the lights. It's tough to see Tanner beating Borg on Har-Tru. If Borg wins, he gets Gerulaitis (whom he famously beat 17 times in a row), and McEnroe in McEnroe's first Major final. Of course, in 1980 and 1981, Borg did play McEnroe in U.S. Open finals, falling in five and four sets respectively. But do those close wins become close losses if it's still on Har-Tru instead of DecoTurf? And we also need to consider that the latter rounds of all these events could look quite different if they're held on Har-Tru. But, in any event, how do we think Borg does on Har-Tru from 1979-1981? Does he win one title? Two? Possibly three? And, if he wins in 1979 or 1980, does he add the Australian Open to complete the CYGS? If Borg wins the 1981 U.S. Open on Har-Tru does he still retire? And, even if he does, do people see that retirement very differently, with Borg going out on top with a Major win over McEnroe instead of the loss he suffered? So, sake of argument, let's say Borg wins the 1979 U.S. Open on Har-Tru, wins the 1980 U.S. Open on Har-Tru, and wins the 1980 Australian Open to take the CYGS. He now has 14 Majors, wins the CYGS, and has an even better conversion rate at Majors. Would that be enough for GOAT status?

text: Is Jimmy Connors actually underrated? I've been watching some old videos of Jimmy Connors recently and it amazes me even now how purely he hits the ball, how beautiful his preparation was and the power, consistency and depth of his shots. In a way I often think Connors is very underrated. The man won 140 plus tournaments in his career and many majors. That's more total tournaments won than Nadal, Federer and Djokovic combined to put it in perspective. And yes I know Connors "officially" won 109 tournaments in his career but the ATP doesn't count many WCT tournaments and other tournaments he won in his career. He played at a very strong level up to a very late age in tennis. He is arguably the best pure ball striker in the history of tennis with super mobility and he is also arguably the greatest service returner in the history of tennis. He also had arguably the greatest backhand in history. One of the reasons I think he is underrated is his relatively small majors total considering how great he was. One of the reasons is that I believe some of the majors were not as important as it is considered today. He didn't played the Australian and the French for many of his prime years but he won tournaments that essentially were majors like the WCT championship and the Year End Masters tournament. Connors won about 82% of his matches for his career. That's incredible considering how many years he played past his best years. He was number one in the world for five years in a row plus he was top ten in the world from 1973 to 1978. He won over 90% of his matches over a five year span and if you don't think that's impressive, Pete Sampras never won 90% of his matches in any ONE year. Connors also played in an extremely competitive time, against older legends like Rosewall, Newcombe, Ashe, Smith and Nastase. He played younger legends like Borg, McEnroe, Lendl, Cash, Edberg, Wilander, Agassi and even Sampras. Do I think Connors is the greatest ever? No I do not but he is one of the few who has a record that you can at least argue reasonably that he is the greatest ever. Please discuss.

text: Making sense of strength of USA tennis and UTR Colleges rely heavily on UTR to recruit players. It’s a good measure of ability and also safe for them. It’s also cheap and easy. You don’t need to physically travel the globe to watch players. There is no “tournament” or playoff for college spots. Players are selected without playing one another. The problem as I see it is UTR is built on a curve. Imagine the science teacher grades essays on a curve, and everyone studies twice as hard. You will have the same distribution or A,B,C etc. So we have about 400 open d1 spots annually. We have about 35 juniors above 12.5 utr. Many of these play internationally. I am just using this number as an example. No matter how hard Americans train, or how good our program is, it’s impossible to have 100 12.5 utr. Or 200. Or 300. There is a soft cap of maybe 25-40. Americans primarily play each other, and often times play other Americans In their geographical area. So when these american players are chosen, other schools need to stay competitive. So they MUST recruit internationally for more 12.5 utr from their ecosystem. Yes, as an individual you can raise your utr with international play, prize money tournaments, etc. But as a whole, it is mathematically impossible for Americans to just “improve” and have 400 junior 12.5 utr and up to fill all the spots. What sort of “fix for American tennis”’ can take place when players are graded on a curve for college spots? Every separate ecosystem will have their own set amount of 12.5 utr whom are going to be selected based on the number

text: Is UTR like pusher? It’s a bit counterintuitive, but it’s actually very true: a pusher or purely defensive player can easily beat an unstable attacking player 6–0, 6–0. For aggressive player, the score is usually much closer, because attacking players also take risks and make errors. My daughter used to be a fully defensive player—she would loop every ball back, keep unforced errors under five per match, and avoid attacking even when she had clear opportunities. The matches didn’t look pretty, but she won a lot, including against many higher-UTR players. But when she started facing stronger opponents (UTR 7+), who could take the ball on the rise, her high, loopy shots became easy targets. She struggled badly in those matches. That’s when we decided to transition her game. Since then, even against players she could previously beat with a purely defensive style, her matches have become much tougher. As a result, her UTR has dropped quite a bit for now..

text: Kill mini tennis/short court warm-up There was a time long ago when the mini tennis/short court warm-up was not an expectation in practice, let alone in USTA tournaments and league matches. It should be obvious that there is no time for wasting effort on how well you can hit little topspin forehands and backhands from the service line when you only have five or 10 minutes for warm-up. The rule is simple, warm up on your own so that when you get an open court for tournament or league play, you can get to a few minutes of groundstrokes, a few minutes of volleys and overheads, and perhaps nine serves. At many of the better-run tournaments, the director or referee will often warn players that they only have one or two minutes remaining of a five-minute warm-up, as it should be. That means league players should also stick to the established norm of a five to 10-minute warm. But I will go further: mini tennis/short court does little to nothing to help the warm-up or practice or match play. What has happened is that over the past few decades, no coach or player wants to be seen out of the norm so all will gullibly swear by it effectiveness, even though at best, it is opinion but more likely a weak defensive echo of someone else's opinion. Swear by it all you want, cite one famous tennis player after another as if their endorsement of mini-tennis or a sports drink is gospel, but mini-tennis/short court is not needed to warm up. Nope, a simple full-court warm-up will do in order to warm up.
label: hot_take

text: Kill the apology racquet/hand raise It used to be good etiquette to raise the racquet or hand after hitting a net cord winner, but over the past few years, the practice has mutated to raise the racquet or hand to express regret at any winner or any opponent mistake. It is annoying at this point, distracting, so I ask that is stop. If you are a good person and player, you don't need to tell us. That said, this practice infected me as well. I hit a winner, I tip my racquet. My opponent double faults, I tip my racquet. So lately, I have been reacting with common sense with my hitting partner friends. I celebrate silently my winners, and I needle my practice partner for giving me a free point, I do all I can to not apologize. We are all trying to win points and the match. However, watch any tournament through this summer, and notice how often the pros, especially the men, are raising the racquet or hand to say sorry for a number of reasons. Get on YouTube and check out all the matches from the 1980s, players were much more honest then, they openly hit at the body and head, and rarely raised the racquet or hand. To be fair, Ivan Lendl raised a racquet a bit in the 1981 Masters after he drilled Vitas Gerulaitis in the forehead at the net. Enjoy hitting winners because you are going to hit a whole bunch of errors, too. Same thing with receiving a double fault, it's all part of the game, so let's stop making these special moments and compete.
label: hot_take

text: Once again, the folly of the 0.5 NTRP = 6-0 6-0 On Saturday, I played in a local inter-club league. This is an open level league with 4 doubles lines per match. The top teams have 5.0 and high 4.5 caliber players. I play for the "B" team for my local club, which is 4.5 and high 4.0 level, and we're in the lower tier of the league. I was playing with another guy from my 4.0 nationals team. We are both 4.0 rated, and we were playing one of the stronger clubs in the league, so I was expecting to use this as a chance to play high caliber competition with little chance to win. Sure enough, we were playing a college kid (said he played club tennis for a Big Ten D1 school, was definitely not good enough for varsity Big Ten tennis) and an older guy, who were both very good. The college kid hit huge shots, but the older guy was the better overall player with a very polished doubles game an no weaknesses. We played really well, my partner had a great serving day, and we only lost 6-4 6-4 (we were only broken once per set, but didn't break and only had 2 break points in the whole match). Out of curiosity, I looked up the people we played in the USTA website just to see if they played USTA and at what level. The older guy was 5.0 rated and only played sporadically because 5.0 league play around here is spotty at best. His 5.0 results were very good, and his last USTA match was in 5.0 nationals a couple years ago, where he won both his matches. The younger guy has played 4.5 since he was a senior in high school and had a 7-3 regular season record and 1-1 playoff record last summer. So, that was a nationals-level 5.0 and a upper echelon 4.5 playing two 4.0s and we played them to 6-4 6-4. Even if we're high 4.0, there's at least a 0.5-1.0 DNTRP difference between us, yet we played to a reasonably competitive score. To be clear, they were never in danger of actually losing even a set, but for those that blindly take the USTA's 0.5 DNTRP = 6-0 6-0 blurb out of context, you are once again entirely wrong. That is NOT the expected results for a 0.5 difference in DNTRP.

So let's start there, where Federer was aged 27 (and already past his prime), Nadal 22, Djokovic 21, and Murray 21 (the latter 3 in their primes or close to it). text: weak era finally solved the statistic is: p_elo - p_bookmaker We convert elo to probability (p_elo) and we convert bookmaker odds to probability (p_bookmaker), calculated at the match level. premise: Bookmaker odds capture the current strength of the matchup. Bookmakers are forward looking…ELO is backwards looking and captures historical performance built up over prior matches. if the elite group's p_elo (#1-#8) runs ahead of p_bookmaker (for #9 seed - #50 seed) on a given match, ELO is more confident than the market. Pooled across many matches, this washes out player-specific noise (injury, one bad day, a hot streak) and leaves something closer to a systemic read: historical ratings aren't reflecting the current competition. A systemic positive difference between top-8 Elo and top 9-50 betting odds across matches indicates the elite tier has likely declined in quality, ELO is overestimating the odds the field has of beating #9-50 seeded players. Caveats: -this doesn't measure the elite era quality in terms of how top seeds fare at beating other top seeds. -The 9-50 group is large enough to assume decent enough uniformity of their level post ‘00s. Some bias may be introduced in very deep eras although would expect it to be rather minimal. data/methodology: matches between top 8 seeds (by year-end rank) vs ranks 9-50 only. matches from 2004-2019 calculated p_elo - p_bookmaker for each qualifying match, linearly decaying weights for year ends 1-8, so the #1 seed counts more than the #8 seed in determining era strength we flag matches where the gap exceeds a threshold (75th percentile of the full sample) and report the % of matches per year that cross it results: ok: 04-08 stronk: 09-12 ok: 13-15 weak: 16-19 discuss.

text: Sinner’s domination of top-10 players has been historically great this year. Dominance of top-10 players: 2026 Sinner vs 1984 Mac vs 2004 Federer vs 1978 Borg. I wanted to look at the .900 club vs top-10 players(minimum 10 matches played). That ruled out a bunch of other incredible runs. 2026 Sinner: 10-1, 1.45 DR, 59.3% games won 1984 McEnroe: 26-2, 62.1% games won 2004 Federer: 18-0, 1.28 DR, 61.6% games won 1978 Borg: 20-2, 65.5% of games won Sinner’s 1.45 DR is by far the highest that I could find vs top-10 players. But his % of games won isn’t quite there. And the DR stat only goes back to 1991. But still. His 1.45 DR vs the top-10 is a massive outlier. I’m always going to pick Mac’s 1984 as the gold standard; mostly due to the insane level of competition that he dominated that year. He was something like 14-1 vs Lendl, Wilander, and Connors. Borg’s 1978 season flies under the radar for some reason. His 65.5% of games won vs the top-10 is absolutely insane. 60% is a historical number. I didn’t even think 65% had ever been approached until I looked this one up. Hard courts are what costed Borg a perfect record vs the top-10. He lost the USO final to Connors while playing with an infected thumb(racket slipped out of his hand several times during that match). And he lost to McEnroe on hard courts. That’s it. He was a perfect 7-0 on carpet and 7-0 on clay, 1-0 on grass, and 5-2 on hard courts. Borg in 1978 was absolutely incredible. This is an ATG season. Fed’s perfect record deserves a huge shout out. Federer’s play on fast hard courts like the WTF in Houston was mind-blowing. He made the WTF courts in Houston look like ping pong tables. To me, I loved watching Fed play on fast hard courts more than any other surface. Sampras vs Federer on fast hard courts would be a dream matchup, perhaps even more than Federer vs Mac on grass. I’ve always said that 2004 was Fed’s best season; mostly because of my own eye test. But his demolition of top players is another big reason why.

text: Rafa’s Surface Disparity “Injury” Record From 2012-2022, this was Rafa’s appearance records in clay to hard masters in masters that were held. Hard Court 38/64 =59.37% Clay Court 30/31 =96.77% This really isn’t spoken about enough. There is absolutely no way this is just coincidence or because Rafa found it physically easier to play on clay. Why do I say this? From 2005-2011, another sustained period Rafa had the following appearance record in masters. Hard court 37/42 =88% Clay court 19/21 =90% To my mind, it’s obvious Rafa systematically prioritised the clay over the hard court from 2012 all the way to the rest of his career. And as a result his overall win% for matches and tournaments are skewed to a higher percentage than they would have been if he had treated the surfaces more equally like Roger and especially Novak over their whole careers.

text: Rosewall > Laver In the Open Era : Rosewall has 4 Grand Slams Laver has 5 (including the calendar year Grand Slam) Pro Slams : Rosewall has 15 Laver has 8 So Rosewall has 19 Majors compared to Laver's 13. It's obvious Rosewall is far more successful. And these are some ways in which he is statistically better : Dominance - Rosewall won 9 consecutive Pro Slams that he participated in. Laver only ever managed 4 Pro Slams in a row and 4 Open Era Grand Slams in a row. His 4 in a row against amateurs isn't comparable. Longevity - Rosewall won his first Major in 1957 and his last Major in 1972. That's 15 years apart. Laver won his first in 1964 and his last in 1969. Just 5 years apart. Versatility - Rosewall has 5 Grasscourt Majors, 5 Claycourt Majors, 5 Indoorcourt Majors, 4 Woodcourt Majors. That's 5-5-5-4. Very balanced, showing he was a versatile player. Laver has 8 Grasscourt Majors, 1 Claycourt Major, 4 Indoorcourt Majors, 1 Woodcourt Major. That's 8-1-4-1. Very lopsided and grass/indoor heavy, showing he was more of a fastcourt player and not as versatile. I think Rosewall is head and shoulders above Laver, in almost every way. I don't even see it as debatable, statistically.

text: Is Elizabeth Ryan the best women's player never to win a singles Major? We've had past threads about the best women's player never to win a Major, with Suková, Shriver, Dementieva, and Fernández usually being toward the tops of those lists. I can't remember anyone mentioning Elizabeth Ryan, but I feel like she has a strong case. Here are her stats: Career record: 1,064-94 (91.9%)​Major finals: Wimbledon 1921, U.S. National Championships 1926, Wimbledon 1930​H2Hs: 7-2 against Molla Mallory (8 Major winner); 5-5 against Cilly Aussem (2 Major winner); 10-11 against Kitty Godfree (2 Major winner); 3-3 against Chambers (7 Major winner); 2-3 against Wills (19 Major winner); 4-0 against Browne (3 Major winner); 2-0 against Wightman (4 Major winner)​Rankings: #1 in ELO in 1920; top 5 in ELO for 11 straight years (1919-1929)​Titles: 214 singles titles; 42 other finals; 17 doubles Majors; 9 mixed doubles Majors​ Starting with that career winning percentage, 91.9% is the second highest in tennis history, behind only Ryan's tormentor Suzanne Lenglen, who was 15-0 against her. It's slightly higher than the winning percentages for Wills (91.8%) and Court (90.9%). Turning to Major finals, Ryan had three, behind only Suková among non-Major winners and tied with Fernández. The difference is that Ryan didn't play either the U.S. National Championships or Roland Garros until 1925/1926, when she was 33/34. Of course, while this deprived her of many chances to win Majors, it might also explain her high career winning percentage. But... Her H2Hs are really solid. Sure, she never could beat Lenglen. But look at her records against the other greats of her era. Winning records against Mallory, Browne, and Wightman. Tied records against Aussem and Chambers. Just one loss under .500 against Godfree and Wills. Turning to rankings, she was #1 in ELO in 1920, when she went 99-5. Other top seasons include 1921, when she went 106-5, and 1925, when she went 101-3, including 2-0 against Mallory. And her 11 year run from 1919-1929 is a model of consistency that would make even Shriver blush. Finally, in terms of titles, 214 is eye popping, even considering the era. According to her NYT obituary, she won a total of 659 titles across singles, doubles, and mixed doubles, including the 17 doubles/9 mixed doubles Majors listed above. Until recently, I had always discounted Ryan, thinking that she had an inflated winning percentage due to not playing great competition. But, as the above H2Hs show, she was a combined 33-24 (57.9%) against Mallory/Aussem/Godfree/Chambers/Wills/Browne/Wightman, who had a combined 45 singles Majors. Overall, it feels like Ryan is unfairly written off as someone who faced weak competition. IMHO, she seems like the best women's player never to win a singles Major.
label: analysis

text: Djokovic and Nadal - Their surface achievements compared through Rafa’s peak years 2008-2014 - who was better on each surface and when. Recent conversations have frustrated me with fellow Federer fans and Nadal fans regarding Rafa’s peak and when Novak actually became the dominant player on tour by becoming conclusively better on 2 surfaces. So this look, only uses Rafa fans’ self proclaimed peak years. Key:- S = Slams, B = Other Big Titles (masters, ATP finals, Olympics) C = Clay, H = Hard, G = Grass Rafa score first, Novak score second. 2008 CS 1-0, CB 2-1, HS 0-1, HB 2-3, GS 1-0 2009 CS 0-0, CB 2-0, HS 1-0, HB 1-1, GS 0-0 2010 CS 1-0, CB 3-0, HS 1-0, HB 0-0, GS 1-0 2011 CS 1-0, CB 1-2, HS 0-2, HB 0-3, GS 0-1 2012 CS 1-0, CB 2-0, HS 0-1, HB 0-4, GS 0-0 2013 CS 1-0, CB 2-1, HS 1-1, HB 3-3, GS 0-0 2014 CS 1-0, CB 1-1, HS 0-0, HB 0-4, GS 0-1 And here is their respective match winning % on each surface each season excluding matches against each other, to show you how good they were on each surface in each period:- Again Rafa score first, Novak second 2008 C 95-94 H 83-79 G 100-83 2009 C 90-89 H 79-82 G NA-78 2010 C 100-83 H 81-80 G 91-75 2011 C 100-94 H 80-90 G 91-90 2012 C 95-94 H 89-91 G 33-80 2013 C 97-84 H 94-94 G NA-86 2014 C 92-93 H 77-87 G 75-88 Nadal was actually winning a greater % matches on hardcourts 11-14 then he was 8-10. It’s just that Djokovic’s improvement was much greater than Rafa’s on this surface and that’s why he overtook him on hard. Grass, Djokovic improved and Rafa pretty much forgot how to play on the surface from 2012. 2008-2010: CLAY: Rafa is hugely dominant on clay, 2 slams to 0 and winning 9 big titles on clay compared to 1 from Novak. 0 seasons where Novak wins more slams or big titles. HARD: Rafa has the edge in slams 2 to 1, it’s 5-5 in big titles, but with an extra slam the advantage goes to Rafa. GRASS: Rafa has a clear dominant advantage 2-0 in slams. Summary:- Rafa has a huge dominance on clay, dominance on grass and a much closer advantage on hard. 2011-2014 CLAY: Rafa stays very dominant on clay, 3 slams to 0 and winning 8 big titles on clay compared to 4 from Novak who cuts the gap in the other big titles ratio from 9:1 to 2:1. HARD: Novak becomes hugely dominant. 4 majors to 1 and 14 other big titles to 3. 4:1 ratio in majors, 5:1 ratio in other big titles. There are 0 seasons where Rafa wins more majors or big titles than Novak. GRASS: Novak has a clear dominant advantage 2-0 in slams. Summary:- Novak has a huge dominance on hard, a clear dominance on grass, and Rafa retains his big dominance on clay. And nothing changed from 2015 onwards apart from Novak becoming even more dominant on hard and grass over Rafa. So once and for all, can some of us cut the BS about when it happened. Novak became a substantially better 2 out of 3 surface player than Rafa in 2011. It’s as conclusive as it gets.
